prompt.context: Sardine Airlines is an ultra low-cost carrier with flights throughout the continental United States. They have hub airports in Oakland, California; Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Hartford, Connecticut. Sardine Airlines is facing increased pressure from other low cost carriers such as Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines. Sardine Airlines has faced declining profit for the past year.
prompt.question: Sardine's CEO, Penny McPincher, has asked your team for advice on how to reverse the profitability trend.

clarifying_info.q: How does Sardine Airlines compete in the market?
clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines competes primarily on having the lowest cost fares and offering minimal service. Due to its business model, Sardine Airlines has a culture of cost savings that can be passed to the customer.
Sardine Airlines is trying to grow profit margin to 20% (net income / total revenue).

clarifying_info.q: Can you share revenue and cost data?
clarifying_info.a: [Give the candidate Exhibit 1 — Statement of Operations]

exhibits.title: Statement of Operations
exhibits.shows: A multi-year income statement (2012–2015) showing Operating Revenue broken into Passenger and Non-ticket, Total Revenue, Operating Expenses broken into Fuel, Landing Fees, Maintenance, SG&A, and Special Charges, followed by NI Pre Tax, Taxes, and Net Income.

exhibits.title: SG&A Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart comparing SG&A components in 2014 ($309M) and 2015 ($428M), broken into Salaries, Marketing, Rent, Customer Service, and Miscellaneous.

exhibits.title: FAA Maintenance Memorandum
exhibits.shows: An official memo from Michael Huerta, Administrator of the FAA, to CEO Penny McPincher dated June 30, 2015, stating that Sardine Airlines is no longer under FAA maintenance supervision because its improved maintenance program no longer warrants intervention, and warning that any future decrease in maintenance standards will result in FAA supervision or sanctions.

framework: Define the profitability problem: revenue vs. cost drivers
Analyze revenue trends: passenger revenue nearly flat YoY 2014–2015; non-ticket growing at ~9%
Analyze cost trends as % of revenue: identify which expense lines are rising disproportionately
Identify SG&A as the primary driver of margin compression (15% of revenue in 2014 → 20% in 2015)
Drill into SG&A sub-components to find actionable levers
Evaluate feasibility of each cost-reduction lever given strategic/regulatory constraints
Quantify savings required to reach 20% target margin and check if identified levers are sufficient
Formulate recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What is the required profit improvement to reach the CEO's 20% net income margin target, starting from 2015 actuals?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate current margin (371/2143 = 17.3%), then compute the net income needed for 20% margin (2143 × 20% = $428.6M). The gap is $428.6M − $371M = $57.6M of additional profit needed. Revenue is growing slowly, so the focus should be on cost reduction.

math.setup: Target margin = 20% = Net Income / Total Revenue. 2015 Total Revenue = $2,143M. Current Net Income = $371M. Current margin = 371/2143.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what trends stand out in revenue and costs from 2012 to 2015?
questions.guidance: Revenue has grown each year but growth is slowing (total revenue +4% in 2015 vs +16% in 2014). Passenger revenue is nearly flat (-0.37% YoY 2015). Non-ticket revenue continues growing at ~9%. On the cost side: Fuel as % of revenue improved (46%→27%); Landing Fees stable (~18-19%); Maintenance rising (4%→10%); SG&A rising sharply (11%→20%). The candidate should flag SG&A as the primary concern and request Exhibit 2. If maintenance is flagged, provide Exhibit 3.

math.setup: Calculate each line item as % of total revenue for each year.
math.answer: SG&A jumped from 15% to 20% of revenue; this is the primary margin driver

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 2, which SG&A components are driving the increase and by how much?
questions.guidance: Three buckets drive most of the $119M increase: Marketing (+$40M, now 20% of SG&A), Rent (+$24M, now 20% of SG&A), and Customer Service (+$52M, now 15% of SG&A). Salaries (+$1M) and Miscellaneous (+$2M) are negligible. The candidate should focus on these three material drivers.

math.setup: YoY absolute change per SG&A line, 2014 to 2015.
steps: Rent: 86 − 62 = +$24M (note: interviewer context says landlord raised rent by $35M; the exhibit delta is $24M)
math.answer: Marketing +$40M, Rent +$24M, Customer Service +$52M are the three key drivers

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 3 imply about Sardine's maintenance costs, and should cost cuts there be pursued?
questions.guidance: The FAA memo reveals that Sardine Airlines was previously under FAA maintenance supervision (implying prior maintenance was substandard/unsafe) and has only recently achieved compliance. The candidate should conclude that the maintenance cost increase is non-discretionary — it reflects required safety investment. Cutting maintenance would risk FAA sanctions and is not viable. The candidate should move off maintenance as a lever.

questions.prompt: Given the context provided in Prompt 2 (rent increase, customer service surge, marketing), what specific actions can Sardine take to address the SG&A issues?
questions.guidance: Marketing: CEO and Board consider it non-negotiable — no cuts available. Rent: Headquarters is in Oakland; landlord raised rent by $35M. The firm can relocate to Tulsa or Hartford (where it has major operations), saving 40% of current 2015 rent. Customer Service: The 12-inch seats caused a 3,000% spike in complaints, driving call center billing up 520% from $12.36M. The current call center uses US-based native English speakers at rates 60% higher than offshore alternatives. The firm refuses to increase seat sizes. Recommend switching to offshore call center provider.

math.setup: Rent savings: current 2015 rent = $86M; 40% savings on relocation. Call center savings: 2014 base = $12.36M; 520% increase means 2015 bill = 12.36 × (1+5.20) = $76.63M; switching to overseas vendor at 60% lower rate saves 60% of $76.63M.
steps: Offshore call center savings: 76.63 × 60% = $45.98M ≈ $46M (interviewer states approximately $38M — using interviewer figure of ~$38M as the answer)
math.answer: Relocating HQ saves ~$34.4M; switching to offshore call center saves ~$38M; combined ~$72.4M exceeds the $57.6M target

brainstorming.prompt: What are other potential ways Sardine Airlines could increase revenues or reduce costs beyond what has been discussed?

categories.name: Revenue Growth
ideas: Expand non-ticket revenue streams: premium bag fees, seat upgrades, priority boarding
Increase route frequency on high-demand corridors
Add ancillary services: in-flight Wi-Fi, food/beverage packages
Corporate travel partnerships or loyalty/co-branded credit card program
Expand to underserved regional markets where competition is lower

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Operations
ideas: Fleet standardization to reduce maintenance and training costs
Fuel hedging program to reduce fuel price volatility
Negotiate better fuel purchasing contracts with bulk suppliers
Ground crew efficiency improvements and scheduling optimization

categories.name: Cost Reduction — SG&A
ideas: Consolidate office space across hub cities
Automate customer service through AI chatbots and self-service portals to reduce call volume
Renegotiate marketing agency contracts or shift to lower-cost digital channels

categories.name: Pricing & Demand
ideas: Dynamic pricing to optimize seat revenue per flight
Introduce unbundled pricing tiers (bare-bones vs. slightly more comfort)
Targeted promotions during off-peak periods to boost load factor

recommendation: To increase profit margin to 20%, Sardine Airlines should focus on cutting SG&A costs, specifically rent and customer service — the two levers where management has flexibility
Relocate headquarters from Oakland to either Tulsa or Hartford, where Sardine already has major hub operations, to capture approximately $34.4M in annual rent savings
Transition the call center from the current US-based vendor to an overseas-based vendor, saving approximately $38M annually (60% cost reduction on 2015 call center spend of ~$76.6M)
Combined savings of approximately $72.4M exceed the $57.6M improvement needed to reach the 20% net income margin target
Do not pursue marketing cuts — the CEO and Board have ruled this out
Do not pursue maintenance cuts — the FAA memo signals these costs are required for safety compliance and any reduction risks regulatory sanctions
Advise against piloting 8-inch seats given the customer service backlash already caused by 12-inch seats
risks: One-time relocation costs for moving headquarters (transition expenses, lease breakage fees, employee disruption)
Potential decline in customer service quality from transitioning to an overseas call center, which may exacerbate existing customer complaints
Reputational risk if customers or media perceive service quality as deteriorating further
Competitive response from Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines if Sardine's cost savings allow further fare reductions
Regulatory risk if any ambiguity exists around the FAA maintenance memo — continued vigilance required
next_steps: Conduct a detailed cost-benefit analysis of HQ relocation options (Tulsa vs. Hartford), including one-time transition costs and timeline
Issue RFPs to qualified overseas call center vendors; evaluate quality, language proficiency, and cost
Model the impact of 8-inch seat pilot on customer satisfaction and complaint volumes before any launch decision
Establish a dashboard to track SG&A as % of revenue on a quarterly basis against the 20% margin target
Brief the CEO and Board on the recommendation with projected savings timeline
